title: CASE OF MARIAN CHIRIȚĂ v. ROMANIA
conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment) (Substantive aspect)
summary: In the case of Marian Chiriță v. Romania, the applicant, Mr. Marian Chiriță, is a Romanian national of Roma ethnic origin who was serving a prison sentence in Romania. The case highlighted the particular vulnerability of Roma detainees, who often face systemic barriers to adequate healthcare in detention, compounding their marginalisation. Mr. Chiriță, suffering from severe heart disease and other chronic conditions, was repeatedly denied timely and appropriate medical treatment while in prison. Despite a final court order in November 2009 requiring his admission to a public hospital for urgent bypass surgery, the authorities failed to ensure he received the necessary care, instead keeping him within the prison health system, which was not equipped for such complex procedures. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court found that Romania had violated Article 3, concluding that the authorities’ failure to provide adequate medical care and to enforce the court order caused Mr. Chiriță prolonged physical and mental suffering. This judgment is significant for Roma and Traveller rights, as it underscores the obligation of states to protect the dignity and health of Roma detainees, a group historically subjected to discrimination and neglect within European prison systems.
